title: Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Background & Summary · Par2】Conventional histology, based on two-dimensional sectioning and staining, remains the gold standard for diagnostic pathology and biological tissue assessment. However, its planar nature inherently limits spatial interpretation, as three-dimensional (3D) morphologies, connectivity, and volumetric relationships between tissue compartments are lost during sectioning1–6. Convoluted structures, complex distributions, and rare pathologic occurrences can be detected and assessed more precisely in 3D data1,4,5. Reconstruction from serial sections is theoretically possible, but in practice, it is labor-intensive, prone to misalignment artifacts, and unsuitable for volumetric quantification across large cohorts7,8. 3D imaging methods overcome this limitation by preserving the spatial organization of tissue microanatomy and enabling quantitative morphometric analyses in a true volumetric context6.

【Background & Summary · Par3】Optical approaches to achieve 3D visualization of biological tissue have been developed7,8. Optical clearing homogenizes refractive indices across tissue components, rendering biological samples transparent and thus more amenable to optical investigation7–10. While these approaches offer excellent molecular specificity when combined with fluorescence labelling, they are limited by antibody penetration and optical scattering11. The clearing process itself can require multiple days to weeks, depending on tissue volume7,8,12. Imaging using light-sheet microscopy can result in anisotropic voxel geometry and depth-dependent signal attenuation13. In addition, quenched and altered autofluorescent signals limit applicability toward clinically processed and archived samples such as formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. Synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography (SRµCT) has emerged as a technology for non-destructive, label-free, isotropic 3D imaging of biological specimens14–17. In contrast to conventional absorption micro-computed tomography, SRµCT leverages phase shifts of coherent X-rays arising from refractive-index variations of materials or tissue compartments, respectively16,18. Thereby, contrast in weakly absorbing specimens can be enhanced18. The three key beam properties, namely high brilliance, coherence, and collimation, enable rapid data acquisition and robust soft tissue contrast without exogenous staining16. Rotation of the specimen of ≥180° yields a projection series for phase retrieval and tomographic reconstruction into high-fidelity 3D volumes16. Moreover, the imaging process is non-destructive, allowing downstream histological, molecular, or multimodal analyses on the same sample19,20. Sample preparation critically affects data quality21. For large or delicate soft-tissue specimens, protocols for sample stabilization, dehydration, and mounting minimize motion, shrinkage, and acquisition-induced artifacts during scans21,22. Therefore, FFPE specimens remain particularly compatible with a downstream multimodal analysis. FFPE tissue is the most widely used format in biobank repositories, making SRµCT a particularly powerful tool for translational research16,23.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methods · Par7】The end-to-end data workflow used in this study is illustrated in Fig. 1. The pipeline comprises sample selection from the biobank, region-of-interest (ROI) definition, SRµCT imaging, and histological processing. Each stage includes dedicated pre-processing and post-processing steps. Together, these steps lead to the final processed dataset used for the analyses presented in this manuscript.

【Background & Summary · Par4】Recently, hierarchical phase-contrast tomography (HiP-CT) has extended SRµCT to intact human organs by combining whole-organ imaging with targeted higher-resolution acquisition19,21. HiP-CT demonstrated organ-to-cellular mapping in intact brain, lung, heart, kidney, and spleen, including quantitative morphometry in situ22,24–27. Such volumetric, non-destructive datasets can bridge anatomy across scales and support disease investigation (e.g., COVID-19 lung pathology)28. The public release of datasets through the Human Organ Atlas demonstrates the potential for reuse and community uptake in research, education, and algorithm development27. By contrast, the current dataset comprises 1.0 mm tissue cores imaged at high resolution. It therefore captures local microarchitecture rather that organ-wide spatial organization. The two approaches are complementary: HiP-CT is suited to multiscale mapping of intact organs, whereas the present core-based workflow supports standardized, high-resolution analysis of pancreatic microarchitecture and its cellular and tissue compartments across clinically characterized cohorts. These developments mark a transition from purely qualitative visualization toward quantitative, standardized 3D morphology as a prerequisite for large-scale analysis and algorithmic interpretation1.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Data co-registration and validation with immunohistochemistry data · Par21】To enable validation of X-ray–based islet segmentation against histological ground truth, two-dimensional IHC sections were co-registered with corresponding virtual slices extracted from the 3D SRµCT volumes. Virtual slices were generated from the reconstructed volumes at orientations and depths matching the physical sectioning planes of the TMAs. In addition, the physical slice thickness from histology sectioning was approximated by generating maximum intensity projections. This ensures direct comparability between the histology and X-ray datasets within the same tissue core. Initial alignment was performed using affine-rigid transformations based on anatomical landmarks, including ducts, vascular structures, and tissue boundaries, in VGSTUDIO MAX 2025.1 (Volume Graphics GmbH / HEXAGON, Heidelberg, Germany). Non-rigid registration was applied to account for deformation introduced during tissue-core sectioning and re-embedding. For the downstream use of the data (in this case, deep learning validation and multi-staining co-registration), non-rigid transformations were performed using Fuxlastix46. Co-registration accuracy was visually assessed by expert users before downstream validation analyses. For quantitative analysis, insulin-stained histological sections were used as a reference for endocrine tissue. Binary masks of insulin-positive regions were generated from the IHC images using a Python script (see section “Code Availability”, binarize_histo.py). Cropped histological slices were processed for intensity thresholding, followed by smoothing as a morphological cleanup step to remove isolated noise and staining artifacts. The resulting binary masks represent regions with detectable insulin expression and were used as an independent validation reference.

【Validation of deep learning-based segmentation on SRµCT data · Par22】For each validated dataset, the segmentation output of the corresponding 2.5D U-Net model was projected onto the histology co-registered virtual slice plane. Validation of automated segmentation was performed using insulin IHC reference data. Validation metrics were chosen according to a previous consensus statement47 and include the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and intersection-over-union (IoU). In addition, true positive regions were defined as insulin-positive areas correctly identified by the segmentation, while false positive regions were defined as segmented areas without a corresponding insulin signal.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · Fig1】Fig. 1 Methodological workflow for multimodal 3D virtual histology and validation. The figure illustrates the end-to-end experimental and computational pipeline, structured according to the BPMN 2.0 standard, with events, activities, gateways, and data objects. Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) pancreatic tissue blocks are first sectioned and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H/E), followed by whole-slide imaging (WSI) and definition of regions of interest (ROI). Cylindrical tissue cores are extracted by punch biopsy, and the tissue block is subsequently resected for documentation and ROI verification. Biopsy punches are mounted for synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography (SRµCT). After SRµCT acquisition and reconstruction, the volumetric X-ray datasets are masked, cropped, and annotated by experts. These annotations are used to train and apply deep-learning segmentation models, yielding multi-label masks of pancreatic microstructures. In parallel, scanned paraffin punches are re-embedded into tissue microarrays, sectioned, and processed for immunohistochemistry (IHC). Binary masks derived from IHC serve as histological ground truth. Finally, segmented 3D SRµCT volumes and histological data are co-registered and merged, enabling multimodal validation of automated segmentation results. The terminal event is met by the generation of a merged, validated dataset for downstream analysis.

【Fig. 2 · Fig2】Fig. 2 Cohort structure. Sankey-style diagram illustrating the cohort composition with 55 tissue cores derived from 32 patients and stratification into clinically defined subcohorts. Individual patient identifiers are grouped by subcohort. Flow widths are proportional to the number of tissue cores, summarizing sample distribution and cohort balance.

【Fig. 3 · Fig3】Fig. 3 Deep-learning-based data analysis and presentation.The figure illustrates the application of the provided SRµCT dataset P_6_10_2 together with the corresponding deep learning–based segmentations. Panel (a) shows the entire FFPE core acquired with SRµCT. Panel (b) illustrates the same core (P_6_10_2) using the deep learning–based tissue segmentation, displaying the tissue (purple) in a cross-section and the endocrine tissue (green). Panel (c) shows the same FFPE core with tissue and background rendered semi-transparent. The endocrine tissue was analyzed using the provided code, which also performs volume calculations and assigns individual islets of Langerhans to distinct colors in the RGB spectrum. Panel (d) shows the same core punch, zoomed out slightly to reveal the surrounding three-dimensional representation. The legend in the lower right applies to panels (c) and (d) and provides information on the actual size of the islets of Langerhans. The scale bar applies to all four panels and represents 500 µm.

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Spatial resolution estimation by Fourier Shell Correlation · Par18】The effective spatial resolution of the reconstructed SRµCT volumes was estimated using Fourier shell correlation (FSC)19,41,42. FSC analysis was performed independently for the four representative datasets used for expert annotation and deep-learning training using custom Python scripts (see section “Code Availability”, mask_crop.py). For each dataset, two statistically independent reconstructions were generated from complementary subsets of the projection data. A cube with an edge length of 1000 pixels in the center of each half-volume was aligned and transformed into Fourier space. FSC was computed as the normalized cross-correlation of corresponding Fourier shells as a function of spatial frequency. The resolution was defined according to the half-bit criterion19,41. The spatial frequency at which the FSC curve crossed the half-bit threshold was converted into an equivalent spatial resolution based on the known isotropic voxel size of 650 nm of the reconstructed volumes.

【Data analysis, annotation, deep learning, data presentation · Par19】After stitching, datasets were masked and cropped using a custom Python script (see section “Code Availability”, mask_crop.py) to reduce the dataset to the tissue volume. 2D-Annotation of target structures was carried out using a combination of the built-in SAM2 tool43 and standard annotation tools in Dragonfly 3D-world (v2025.1; COMET Technologies Canada Inc., Montreal, Canada). The islet annotations were generated by three experts. Each expert performed the annotations independently. No disagreement resolution procedure was required, as the islets of Langerhans could be clearly identified in the X-ray data by all annotators. Annotations were generated on two-dimensional image slices within defined regions of interest (ROIs). These annotated ROIs are provided as individual annotation files in the corresponding annotation folder of the data repository36. The annotation of the X-ray tomography data was performed prior to validation with the corresponding histological and immunohistochemical images. Thus, the IHC data were not used to guide the manual annotation process. Instead, histology and immunohistochemistry were subsequently used to validate the X-ray-based annotations. In total, four classes were annotated using the segmentation wizard tool (namely, (i) endocrine tissue/islets of Langerhans, (ii) exocrine tissue, (iii) paraffin-filled space, (iv) masked background). For each of the four example datasets, a separate 2.5D U-Net was trained from scratch using ten initially annotated planes44. A 2.5D U-Net segments a target image slice using information from that slice together with adjacent slices, thereby incorporating limited three-dimensional context while retaining a two-dimensional network architecture. With this, it is superior to standard 2D U-Net networks while limiting computational requirements and processing time. Following the initial training phase, preview images for up to 30 additional new ROIs were generated for each dataset, manually annotated or refined, respectively, and subsequently incorporated into a second iterative training cycle, resulting in approximately 40 total training annotations. Slices for the initial annotation round were selected randomly. Within these slices, ROIs were selected deliberately to obtain a balanced representation of the four segmentation classes. For the subsequent iterative training round, preview ROIs were placed in regions containing as many of these classes as possible, allowing further annotation and refinement of class boundaries. Thus, annotation sampling combined random slice selection with targeted ROI selection rather than a predefined, evenly spaced sampling scheme along the volume depth. Annotations were generated separately for each example dataset and were not pooled across clinical subgroups. After the second training, the trained 2.5D U-Net was applied to the respective dataset from all three spatial orientations (x, y, and z). The three masks derived from the three orientations were subsequently combined into a single multi-label mask. Further processing steps were then applied, namely binarization, morphological closing, smoothing, removal of small objects, and labelling of islets of Langerhans based on their size using ascending grey values. These processes were implemented in an all-in-one script (see section “Code Availability”, DL_postproc.py), allowing each intermediate step to be adjusted to the respective use of the output. The individual steps are separated into script cells and can therefore be processed independently. The data presented here were processed using the Spyder IDE (v6.1.0, Python 3.12.11, 64-bit). Processing a complete volume requires approximately 256 GB of RAM. The main sources of memory demand are full-volume annotation and inference in Dragonfly 3D World and the simultaneous loading and fusion of three complete prediction masks generated along the x-, y-, and z-axes in DL_postproc.py. Memory requirements can be reduced by chunk-wise processing, by restricting inference to one or two spatial orientations, or by using alternative deep-learning software with a more memory-efficient implementation. Restricting inference to fewer spatial orientations, however, may increase direction-dependent segmentation artifacts. The following parameters were used for the creation of the network, annotation, and training of the deep learning network: Input slice count: 3, depth level: 4, initial filter count: 64, batch size: 64, patch size: 64,64,3, maximum epoch number 100, loss function: cross entropy, optimization algorithm: adadelta, early stopping: 15 epochs, unweighted, validation split 20%. Model training and inference were performed on a Linux workstation equipped with a dedicated NVIDIA GPU. 3D visualizations were performed using VGSTUDIO MAX 2025.1 (Volume Graphics GmbH / HEXAGON, Heidelberg, Germany). The 2.5D U-Net models were trained independently from scratch for individual example datasets to demonstrate the segmentation workflow. They were not optimized for cross-dataset or cross-cohort generalization and are not provided as pretrained starting models for adaptation to new datasets. Figure 3 depicts an exemplary dataset after deep-learning-based segmentation. Further a video animation is provided in the data record36.
